game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'm speechless as in what to say for this game, since the entire story totally got me so hard that I'm quite sad it's >only< 5 hours long.

I had quite high expectations, considering the price of the game and the game's length, and I'm very happy to say that Orwell didn't disappoint, not even a little. Episode 1, which is also included in the demo is very short and serves more like a "tutorial" than actual gameplay, and after completing it I was afraid that the rest would look similar - nothing like that, all other 4 episodes were so intense and well-written that I immediately went back to my previous happy state and enjoyed my fun.

And believe me - I hate all sort of VNs and games with huge amount of text, they're usually boring for me and I quickly lose my interest, that's why I was a bit sceptical at first whether I'm going to enjoy Orwell, but I decided to go with it due to a nice -43% (bundle) discount, and I can say that the experience is well worth the money, even at full price.

You should DEFINITELY grab the game if you're interested in all sort of government spying on people, but apart from that it'd be also interesting position for people interested in "working" for government in general, doing detective work, connecting various pieces together and enjoying awesome story. In fact, the story is the most polished thing in the entire game, and it's alone worth the time and money spent on the title, that's why I'd recommend this title even for people that expect more gameplay than reading, such as myself.

From the bad things, the game can seem a bit too "casual", especially for more oldschool gamers like myself - I'd appreciate difficulty setting that would turn off highlighting relevant facts, and definitely allow to jump onto conclusions with only half-available data. Don't get me wrong - the game is awesome and those are not any crucial things that would heavily affect the gameplay, but I kinda miss the option of actually "losing", by jumping onto false assumption and getting fired. Losing should definitely be an option here.

Overall, I really enjoyed my time, this is at least a 9/10 from me - missing point only for being too casual, although that didn't stop me from enjoying the awesome story that the devs coded for me, since I had a lot of fun. I can definitely recommend the title to everyone!

---

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Welcome to Orwellian Big Brother where every action by every citizen of "The Nation" is captured and recorded, and where citizens can be arrested for even the slightest transgression or declaration of anti-Orwell thoughts against The Nation.  You have been recruited by the government as one of its anonymous investigators who must dissect pertinent data and upload this to the government affiliate working with you to prevent a series of terrorist attacks that have been taking place.  Your affiliate can only act on the information you provide (they have no access to the information you have) so your choices matter!

The interface is a joy: very simple and clean, everything very obvious, and the game leads in with a simple tutorial to introduce you to your three tools of Orwell.  On one side of the screen you can open a person's profile to see what information you've gathered on them, and on the other will be their calls messages and mail, with potentially-relevant text highlighted in blue for you to choose whether to add to a person's profile (it cannot be undone if you make a mistake).  You will have to discern who's telling the truth or not, and sometimes you don't have enough information to be 100% sure.  Drag information to a person's profile to attach it to them, and hope you've made the right decision because there is no way to undo this action.

The game would best be described as a combination of simulation, visual novel and point-and-click, but it carries none of the downsides of these games.  Any reading to be done is short, brief and well written, it's really simple to play, and what you can click on is limited to small nuggets of information that the Orwell system deems potentially relevant (and you must decide whether this will help or hinder the government in thwarting the terrorism).  It's not a difficult game, but it's gripping and all too easy to implicate the wrong individual.  At the end I saw the mistakes I'd made.  The best of it is that I somehow suspected that some information was not right as I was playing, but felt compelled to upload it anyway!  My bad!  Replayability is there because there are different outcomes along the way.  The ending is huge but I cannot tell you a thing about it without spoiling the game, but it is worth reaching.

And the soundtrack is amazing.  It's the first time I've ever bought a soundtrack for a game!

If you're unsure, there is a separate playable demo (that's what convinced me to buy the game) and I'm so glad I did.  Yet another great hit for an Indie team who also made the marvellous Hacknet game.  I can't wait to see what Osmotic Studios produce next.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Big Brother watches you. That’s what they told us back in the days, when it was just some kinda fiction and a fantastic story. Now, in our present times this issue has become like a real problem, especially for someone who believes, that their lives are important as hell and like to play a private card all the time. 

The government can learn about you literally everything, thanks to social media, your online purchases, all the cameras hanging around the city, watching at you, information you provide to your employers when you attend to job, mobile phones you use with a GPS modules, etc. 

It can be a problem for lots of people, especially for some who is paranoid and doesn’t seem to be busy all the time with any kind of work (because, otherwise, they wouldn’t have time for these kind of thoughts). On the other hand, it can be really helpful to identify a threat and prevent some kind of tragedy from a single murder to a massive terrorist attack.

Orwell try to develop this idea. In this game, which presents as a visual novel with its own dystopia universe, you have to identify the threat. You will do this with the help of Orwell, a program, created for surveilling the citizens. The whole job starts when system marks someone as a potential threat and you have to investigate that person. Usually, it all starts kinda mild and innocent - you check the public records and information, that does not require you to spy on someone or even hack it - you will check newspapers, police records, maybe some websites. However, in most situations it’s not enough and you have to dig deeper, checking private emails, phonebooks, chat logs, listening to phone calls all other kind of intrusion to private life.

So,what’s the whole point of the game? While you checking on person’s information - Orwell will highlight the most important parts, regarding your investigation. And your task is to gather all of them into one piece for every profile, every person. If you are doubt in the information you’ll have to disable it, or simply ignore it. For example you found a statement about your victim in some kinda boulevard newspaper - definitely not trustworthy source and if it conflicts with another info you found earlier it will be highlighted with a yellow color. So, it’s up to you, to choose where is the truth and where is the misleading information. But you should keep in mind, that you are the one who is responsible for what will happen next to this person, so be responsible for your actions.

And that’s what made Orwell so interesting to me - I literally wanted to find the real truth, you know, to investigate this to the fullest. I never had this feeling, like yeah yeah yeah whatever, I put this metadata here, this one there, oh, a conflict? Lol, whatever, just let me finish this game. No, it wasn’t this case. I felt like I was so into the cases, to understand, either I am dealing with a real threat, a terrorist, or maybe we just ran into something really serious, where someone tries to set up a complete innocent guy and maybe I should pay more attention here and re-check all the profiles. So, Orwell is more about investigation and your ability to read between the lines where it’s needed.

At this point, some of the players will understand that this is not their type of game. Like it or not, but you seriously can’t control the situation, you can’t change something, can’t help to prevent the damage, which is about to happen. You just simply have to put facts in a right place with a right persons and listen to the comments of your mentor Symes. That guy is simply ridiculous. It starts as a tutorial guy at the start of the game, who has to show you all the basics and teach you how to play, and then after that it stays there for the game to react on your actions. Basically, it doesn’t have any access to the information you gathered, so it can only comment on the newest information you provided and by these comments you have to understand either you move the right or a shallow way. 

Orwell is definitely a blast. It has this unique kind of a gameplay with its deep idea and rich stories for someone, who truly values games as a real art. The combination of twists, turnabouts and all these thrilling moments make this game a great place to spend a few hours, maybe dozens of hours, if you will feel like having more than one run to reveal all the achievements and endings. 

Okay, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:

+ Conspiracy theory lover
+ Love the idea of investigating and matching data and clues into one piece 
+ You want to entertain yourself in a great story game for at least few hours
+ Like to dig to the bottom to find out who is who
+ Fan of dramatic stories with its twists, thrilling moments and surprises

Recommend to avoid if you:

- Don’t get the idea of visual novel
- Not a fan of all these talks that government spy on you and we are all under control.  

Enjoy!

[h1]Overview:[/h1]
Orwell takes place in a distopian near future in the fictional city of Bonton in The Nation. Orwell is the codename of a vastly advanced surveilance system. They outsource investigations to outsiders of the nation - you! It is your task to spy on suspects and inform the government of what is going on. Basically, you roleplay as "Mr. FBI Man".

[h1]The Pros:[/h1]
[list]

There are also three endings (more on that later).

[*][b]Some Replayability[/b] - Every chapter has a few endings (usually two or three). After you finish the game, you may choose to replay starting from any chapter (subsequent ones are erased). game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I must say I never heard from that game, after it pops up on Steam at its release date.

And I'm suprised to say, that this game catched me aloen by its name!

I awaited a Big Brother game ... and I got a Big Brother game ... a game, where you can be Big Brother yourself.

You take control of a new surveilance system called Orwell to find the people responsible for a terror bombing.
Fot that you can check websites, 'listen' to calls and chats and search through phones and computers.

Pros:
- Easy to learn gameplay
- Fitting graphic style and background music
- Good story
- 'Just one more minute/level/stage'
- Different endings and outcomes of story parts

Neutral:
- 4-6 hour for a single walkthrough
- Balanced 'Cliché' and 'Suprised' moments/characters

Cons:
- A bit to simple gameplay (there are only some situations, where it is a bit hard to decide between different choices)
- No 'dead ends'
- Linear story progress

As this game offers its first (of five) episodes for free as a demo (works also as a tutorial), you can easily test out, if you like its gameplay. The initial price of around 10 € is very fair, so do the devs a favor if you like the demo and buy it directly. ;)

I really hope the devs use the base concept/gameplay for some more games! I really like that detective style of conecting clues. But at the same time I hope they expend the concept with video footage to analyze, dead ends, more conflicting clues.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A narrative-driven game, Orwell puts you in the role of a government agent spying on unuspecting citizens' private life in order to maintain peace, law & order. Although, contrary to the inspiration of its namesake, the dystopian world of the videogame doesn't reach the extreme attitudes of "1984" of banned art, love and emotions, but is focused mostly on addressing the issue of abuse of privacy in the name of stability and fighting crime.

In all honesty I hadn't really paid attention in the description and the details of the game and I thought I would have control over a much larger variety of random citizens and decide their fate in unrelated cases, but instead I got involved into a much more story-focused game, sort of a political thriller, where you , the player, much investigate the online presence and phone calls of a group of suspects to decide who is responsible for a series of bombings, with the suspects soon becoming more of a "main/supporting cast" entagled in this one single case . However, my false expecattions didn't hinder my enjoyment of the game as it proved equally fun and interesting.

As for the gameplay, it mostly consists of you reading articles, browsing sites or hacked computers and recorded discussions, uncovering clues that open new places and suspects to investigate but it can feel a little hand-holding especially in the early parts of the game where there is really little to do other than adding all the automatically selected useful information to each suspect's profile and only towards the second half and the end of the game does it provide a little bit more challenge and interesting tougher choices. The outcome can slightly change depending on your actions and the information you provide, although sometimes the game does not exactly make its intentions clear - does it expects you to be good at your job (and the game itself)? Or are you supposed to be a buffoon and ignore vital information about a person's physical and mental health? 
in the second part and especially towards the end of the game where the mechanics shine, it becomes much more interesting and it does a much better job presenting theses questions where the stakes are higher and giving you choices that matter much more and i wish I could see more of this intense decision-making more in the early part.

In terms of graphics i think it's pretty clear that this game will appeal to those who do not need fancy graphics but are fans of endless text boxes. The presenattion is quite good with presenting a dystopian version of the internet and social media,
the artstyle is quite appealing with stylized polygonal semi-realistic pictures and thanks to the story-driven nature of the game, a moody soundtrack that ramps up the intensity when major twists and revelations happen.

So overall, perhaps not as deep of a political/"FBI" simulation as it could have been, focusing more on telling a story, Orwell at least succesfully achieves its goal, to present a thought provoking discussion about government surveillance and the grey area surrounding it - a world that isn't always easy to separate into "good" and "bad" guys and where the ends don't always justify the means. Or do they?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b] Orwell [/b]

First of, the game "Orwell" is based on the worldwidly popular novel "1984" by George Orwell, whose surname was picked as the game title and which is set in a totalitarian surveillance state. The game is one of the few games that are being released these days that feature unique gameplay and new ideas, although it's not as popular as it would deserve to be. I, however, bought this game during a recent Steam Sale because it struck my eye and I was interested in this.

[h1] What is Orwell and how does it work you ask? [/h1]

Well, in general, "Orwell" is a game where you're supposed to stop crimes with the use of the new software called "Orwell" in a world that is set in our present. You were the chosen one for the new job as a government agent, alone and in charge of "Orwell". Your only direct communication is "Sykes", another agent speaking to you over a one-way-channel and evaluating your actions and decisions. At first, you're being introduced by a short cutscene about an incident that has just happened: a bombing. Now, your task as an anti-crime agent is to find out who committed the crime and later on arrest him or her. At first, you as the "Orwell"-Agent can observe target people (you start with one that was quite obvious in the opening) with the help of 3 programs: the Reader, something to browse news and websites with, the Listener, to eavesdrop on target people once you've collected their number, and finally the Insider, where you can actively browse through the target's personal computer, once again if you collected a certain data. At first you should be browsing through their "Timelines", a website that is similar to social media that we have, e.g. Facebook and Twitter, collecting basic information of them, something like their name, address, birth date and so on. These information are "datachunks" that you can upload to "Orwell" to fill out the targets profile, but you must be careful, as you will not be able to remove data once uploaded. You will get to know your target pretty fast pretty soon as you can observe everything they do online. Later on, there will be so-called "conflicting datachunks", which include at least 2 datachunks. If you choose one datachunk out of the conflicting pair and upload it, the other datachunk will be disabled, so you have to choose wisely once again. If you've done everything right and chose after your liking you will soon arrest your first suspect, great job! After successfully managing a day, you "log off" of "Orwell" and end your day, your work is over for today. As you progress through the episodes, you'll quickly realize how complicated your "first tutorial task" in your new job get and how everything is connected to each other, but I don't want to spoil all your fun.

"Orwell" features 5 episodes for one price in total, releasing 1 each week, and as of 11/11/2016, 4 episodes are already out.

[h1] Do I like it? [/h1]

I definitely do. It's not a very gameplay intensive game, but rather a point and click/drag game, with a bit of thinking involved, however, I think it's very relaxing and it features a packing story. Although, to fully understand the story you have to read everything you find, or you will only get half of the story, which is why I usually need around 90 mins for a full episode, decision making included. The game devs had a really great idea for a new video game and it's almost a bit frightening to decide, whether a person is guilty or not, only based on online data and the game also once again brings up the controversy about surveillance by the government, even in the most private sectors. I mean, you can read what they write to their closest friends and listen to their phone calls. Nonetheless, it's a very innovative game that I really enjoyed, also the soundtrack of the game fits the situation very well and overall, for a 10$ game, "Orwell" is a master piece. I really hope they release a second part of the game or more episodes.

I definitely RECOMMEND the game, and if you're still a bit unsure, you can still try the demo and see for yourself, before you make a decision.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell stars you, the player, as an investigator in the Nation's (a stand-in for an unholy almagamation of the United States and the United Kingdom) new, government-ordained spying programme. Your job is to investigate suspected terrorists and cherrypick data you've acquired via researching the Internet and spying directly on their conversations, phones, and computers. You upload these data modules to the Orwell database and help construct a profile of these suspects that your advisor (who can't see your research sources in an effort to maintain some sort of ethical loophole) then uses to report back to the authorities, thus causing your actions to have potentially devastating consequences.

I've seen a few people complain about the gameplay--you are, essentially, dragging these data modules from one part of your screen to another (and, frustratingly, it can take a few clicks to get hold of them), which sounds unexciting on paper. But the story is compelling, and it's through this (slightly repetitive and boring) gameplay that you unlock the story, which can branch depending on which data you upload to Orwell. Some of it you have to, some of it you don't--and some of it you can use to alter the perception of certain suspects by picking which element of contradicting data you want to show to the advisor. 

The game does a very good job of highlighting how people become complacent with this level of privacy invasion--I've seen complaints of the game handholding you throughout, but, in my opinion, this helps you to slip into the mindset of uploading whatever data you come across, mindlessly painting suspects as victims because it's what your advisor wants of you. It wasn't until the end of my first playthrough that I realised how much damage I'd caused by providing evidence to suggest that innocent people were guilty of crimes they hadn't committed, and how many of the characters I'd either had arrested or killed via my actions of "innocuously" collecting their data. Which I guess is what the game wants you to do, particularly on a first playthrough.

That's not to say I don't have complaints. The game wants you to play multiple playthroughs, even if only to collect all of the achievements (most of which can be acquired in two playthroughs; two require a third, or replaying chapters on one of your profiles). Different actions have different outcomes and dialogue, and that produces slightly new scenes to watch (or, really, read). The problem is that the texts and calls you have to monitor can be so tediously long, particularly with little deviation--the last chapter has one that's just about shy of 10 minutes, and you can't do anything but sit and let it play. There's no option to skip the scene. 

I've also seen a few people complain that the game thinks people can never lie or exaggerate, which I assume refers to options where you can report suspects for having outspoken anti-government tendencies... but again, I think this is overlooking what the game wants you to consider. 

I highly recommend Orwell, although I bought it in the Humble Bundle and so bought it for much cheaper than its standard price--and I've already collected all the achievements in just over 6 hours of play, which isn't quite a £1 = 1 hour of playtime at its normal price. It's obviously not a game that's appealing to everyone, but I do think for those that like immersive visual novels with political themes (and that's essentially what it is), you'll enjoy Orwell.

Wow. What an amazing visual novel.

Orwell begins as a simple story about an investigator following up on a crime, but deviates into a darker story asking the player if what is for the greater good truly is ethical.

There are a few choices that will change the story significantly, and these choices will create different endings, allowing you to play through the story a few times as different investigators before the game truly "ends" so you can get the whole story.

The only con, a large one in my opinion, is that the game babies you and holds your hand. All answers are highlighted to you. Large red (!) signs appear when there is a pertinent piece of information in that story. NON-STORY SPOILER: [spoiler]At the later end of the game, you are limited on how much information you can process, meaning there is literally no skill or real cognitive function required to do your detective work.[/spoiler] For a game that has the feeling of a detective thriller, you are practically on rails to what is already being laid out for you.

Overall, this is a masterpiece of a novel, it emulates the fearmongering that comes from modern technologies, and has the potential to give you goosebumps from the twists and turns you, the lone investigator finds on the trail. While there are a couple choices that cement the final ending, the majority of the game is spelled out for you, but that's okay, this is an amazing story and worth the hand-holding.

While there are a couple choices that cement the final ending, the majority of the game is spelled out for you, but that's okay, this is an amazing story and worth the hand-holding.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is pretty fascinating, and I am looking forward to the next episodes (this is being released in episodes, bit by bit). Basically, you are being "Big Brother", hacking into personal files, browsing social media sites in order to solve and prevent crimes. 

Surely, there is a pretty obvious message here, which might be a bit too moralistic for some, but then again, I find it fascinating how you can actually upload unclear information (which is in conflict with another bit of information) and thereby push the investigation into the wrong direction.

Example: One guy mentions "torture", but didn't mean actual physical torture, but more like "it was torture to wait", more like in a fun way. However, if you pull that term and upload it, you will convince your superiors that the person is actually into torturing other people, thereby painting a totally wrong picture, distorting the facts. 
Which is what actually happens a lot, not only on the web, irl. 

The game has a certain indie, Papers Please type vibe... the focus here is on the storyline and your activities, and I think it's quite fascinating. The devs did well, letting you browse websites, hack into chats, wiretap phones, hacking desktops. Sure, it will eventually feel a bit "on rails", as you basically look for bits marked in blue and upload them, progressing the story with that, and the relevant bits are the only ones you can use and upload... so the game kind of leads you by the hand. All you do is read and scroll, find the info, drag it to the upload queue. 

However... I do think that a) if you bother to read what is going on, it might actually make you think a bit, and b) the story is pretty interesting, and I can't wait to see where all this leads. Really like the periodic release... every week, there is a new episode, which you are being told about by email. 

In a nutshell - this is a rather interesting little game with some very cool ideas. It might make you think about the story, government involvement, whether the end always justifies the means, and you might ponder who is right and who is wrong in this story. 
There are some technical problems (for example, if you play this on two different devices, you might run into a problem with starting the game on one of them), but the devs are looking into any problem and are clearly communicating what is going on - nice job there. 

Bottom-line
Great little game, eager to see more of it. Quite a bit of reading involved, but this game will make you think, it's an interesting take on the whole idea of Big Brother is watching you, and is quite well executed. 

So far: 7.5/10, score will probably go up once more episodes are released

review_text_raw:
so I just blasted through this in a single sitting, and I have thoughts:

+ looks great, runs smoothly.
~ I am indifferent regarding the music. it's pretty forgettable, but it's not bad by any stretch otherwise.
+ the sound effects are nice, on the other hand.
+ the story has some pretty great twists and turns that are really unique.
+ the ending I got was incredibly satisfying, and I appreciate being allowed to side with either Thought or The Nation (I don't think that's a spoiler, this wouldn't be a very good story-driven, "choices matter" game if it didn't have multiple endings). for those who have played the game, I sided with Thought because not only do I agree with them, but also because I found them to be written in a nuanced way, that they were in the right as far as the narrative framing is concerned, and I thought that it was more interesting to try and cover for them, rather than obeying the fascists calling the shots. if you sided with The Nation for whatever reason, it's definitely worth trying Thought's ending, because it's morbidly hilarious what the final nail in the coffin you use is.
- without spoiling the ending, I have a few narrative problems which are just... not great to see? for starters, two members of Thought are giving their options for what they think you should do, but then they refer to the wrong one as their plan (ex. you can do my plan of going to the store, or the other one of staying home--but they're mixed up). they also seem to immediately learn complex concepts you had to be taught in the tutorial, like, immediately. one of them is tech savvy enough for me to buy it, but the other one isn't and they're the one who name-drops this hyper-specific jargon they shouldn't know. while this does not ruin my enjoyment of this story (hence my recommendation), it feels like there was a bit of a rush, where the ending goes.

overall, pretty damn intriguing, and it's not like a lot of media as of late which invokes George Orwell's legacy without truly understanding who he was as a person. that's enough for me to give it some level of praise.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TBH, the only reason I finally ended up playing this game over everything else in my backlog was because Gabe Newell said in an interview that he really liked the game.

I liked it too.  I would put the genre closest to this game as a "choose your own adventure" Visual Novel, but without a lot of the VN tropes.

To complete the game is about 5-6 hours. You serve the role as "investigator" and find information on suspects involved in crimes.  Another government official makes arrest decisions based on the information that you choose to (or not to) give him.  You cannot directly communicate with this official, only send him certain pieces of information.

This creates an interesting dynamic. You can present misleading evidence to get people arrested, or you can try to protect those who you think are not troublemakers. You feel like you have a lot of power, but at the same time, you'll often have information misinterpreted. A complaint that I have is that sometimes, certain pieces of information seem completely irrelevant, but are needed to be sent to progress the story. At some points I just found myself essentially uploading everything to make the plot advance.

At certain points in the game you'll be given a choice between 2 conflicting pieces of evidence, where you can only upload one. Sometimes, it was completely unclear which evidence was the "truth". However, other times, I was able to take a logical guess as to what was correct based on other information I had found.

Supposedly, there are multiple endings based on the decisions you make (I have not replayed the game yet). I elected to NOT savescum to get the most desirable outcome (though I think my run was mostly clean), and I highly suggest you don't either. Believe me, it's more !!!FUN!!! that way.

As a whole, it's a very good game with a couple of flaws. Worth buying on a sale. Probably not worth full price unless this type of game interests you.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game proves that you dont need fancy graphics for an immersive gaming experience. 

Orwell forces you to rethink the ideas of government, control, surveilance and the right to go : FK YOU; all presented inside the framework of the paranoid dystopian world originally created by George Orwell back in 1948.

Orwell, however is a modern, slick version of Oceania, in which you play a state agent gathering information on citizens in a world that is under perpetual surveilance.  Your role is to select relevant data bites to pass onto a computer system  designed to identify potential threats to the Nation's status quo. 

Where 1984 is a distant dystopia that can likened to far off places like North Korea,  the world of Orwell is far more like the very one we live in. Where the state operatus of Oceania is something that is menacing, power hungry and paranoid, the shades of powerplay in this world is deceptively bright, fresh and friendly, yet equally suspicious and potentially sinister. 

As you gather information you become acutely aware of your own actions and how they potentially affect the lives of the citizens you scrutinize, as you decide which bytes of information will be passed on and which will be hidden.  There are occasions where you will find contradictory information, presenting opposing beliefs, yet easily accepting the vailidy of both in your mind simultaneously.  However, unlike reading Orwell, and having the answers written out for you, here you are  co-conspirator in Big Brother. You start to question the ideas around good and  evil and discover things that potentially, are both.

The concept of the game is as fascinating as the mind games you start playing with yourself as you potentially prosecute or persecute citizens in a world where freedom and control are at constant odds with one another. 

There are more episodes to come,  and the final verdict will not be out for a while, but so far it is a unique and intriguing experience. Possibly the most rewarding asect about the game, is not the game itself, but the things you start to question, even when not playing the game. Though the brilliance of 1984 is in a league all by itself, there is no doubt that this games manages to bring the message in a far more suble way, and succeed in making it relevant to the world we live in today.

That in itself makes for unique and rewarding gameplay, and it would not be outrageous to suggest that Orwell breaks new ground  in the story/novel game genre.

On the flipside, the game is a little too easy, too much handholding and very linear, and the excecution, though good, could have been a lot better. 

HIghly recommended if you are an Orwell fan, even more so if you know little or nothing about 1984.

The game still has new tricks to teach you even in later stages, as you realize exactly how much you can do, and how it mimics real life. The "interface" for the game is itself a computer screen. review_text_raw:
[Spoilers included]

I received the game as a gift and played it almost immediately. Interface was nice a little bit confusing at first, but Symes helped me out for the first part. Story turns very dark very quickly. Over time, a feeling of dread overwhelms me as I submit a vital-looking datachunk to be processed by Orwell. What feels real is how the use of hyperbolic sentences and phrases in the media, usually for comedic effect, can inadvertently be twisted into something that can target you as a threat to the government (case in point, Juliet talking about how Cassi 'tortures' her with muffins/cupcakes, and Symes believing 100% that Cassi indeed tortures Juliet). Scary to think how it would be in the real world.

This game has me reeling. As a fan of Orwell, especially 1984, this feels like a dream. I'm sad it wasn't longer, or that it just follows one track. It reminds me of Papers, Please, with the screening and processing and comparing of vital information. So I was kind of expecting literally screening suspicious targets in the whole country. Then again, the Thought arc was very well-thought out. Again, however, I didn't expect it to end so abruptly on the 5th day. Was hoping for more.

That twist during the conference call was great, but too convenient. The least suspected was the mastermind after all. But why? Were they romantically involved? Were there any signs of fanaticism, obsessive behavior? Don't get me wrong, I love how this played into the story. Just wondering if it's all to convenient for the plot so as to completely throw the investigator off.

Few technical issues, such as the dialogue boxes of the advisors (Delacroix/Symes) sometimes slow down the entire game. During chapter 5, while processing the last 4 datachunks before the call, Delacroix says a reminder and my game just bugs to oblivion. I can't see her message bubble, I can't click on anything. Not to change tabs, heck not even to bring down the main menu of the game. Had to quit the game and open again, thankfully it doesn't restart at the beginning of every day if you quit midway through a chapter, else I'd have never finished it. 

7.2 hours played, 2 endings down. Highly recommend and would get Orwell: Ignorance is Strength.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Point-and-drag game that managed to strike me into deepest psychological state of mind.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a game where you play as an investigator hired outside the Nation. Your task is to discover a crime detail by searching from suspects' background information which you can gather around the web, to be later uploaded into Orwell security program. You will be accompanied by a single adviser in your every work session, their task will revolve around information that you put into Orwell, for them to act based on your input.

The game sets you into the day at the time a bombing is occurred at a public place. Your first day would revolve around investigating who's behind this bombing. You could work all-day long if you want and maybe put all the datachunks - highlighted information - available into Orwell [spoiler]since you are not "timed" until Episode 5[/spoiler], easy as is. But of course, the common ground is to double-check whether a datachunk is valid to your investigation, or they were there only as mere decorations of information scattered freely on web. Your understanding of validity will be tested, well, more or less.

The music managed to keep me into focus, with not too over-exaggerated tunes (listened to them on Spotify and looped them for some time). There are some tense moments - indicated by shock-therapy tune - where you have to choose which info is MORE valid among the other. You will be the judge of things revolving around the web information, but you know what to do. You have been trusted by the Nation to work with them, but are they trusted enough? Theoretically, they should be, giving the ability to build this seemingly-flawless program where you could uncover the truth of these people you're given task to keep an eye on.

Finishing the game, I'm telling you, they indeed work like a charm. Too well.

Oh, also low poly art-style. New term and style to adore in general.

Nitpicks that I have after discussing this with a fellow online investigator:
- I don't have any complaint for the mechanics, but I was hoping we could select our own datachunks instead of being presented in-game. [i]Then again it would be possibly overkill.[/i]
- Having voice actors for the call sessions would be nice, [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/][i]but then it was covered in the sequel which I have yet to get into.[/i][/url] So giving that one a pass.
- Calls and ongoing chats cannot be skipped during episode replay. I don't see a button or tutorial to archive the calls for later... [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/][i]in which they covered this in the sequel, too.[/i][/url] This kills the will to replay the game under the same save file due to inefficiency, [i]unless it's not meant to punish the replayability?[/i]
- I read this somewhere, but calls and chats would start to roll AFTER we clicked on their names. Even when you left the game for coffee or lunch, it won't play until you click on it - making them "the most tolerate group of terrorists one has to deal with". [spoiler]The only uncontrollable moment is on the last episode's final call.[/spoiler]
Keep in mind I didn't need these to be implemented in the game - as they're all already covered in the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/633060/Orwell_Ignorance_is_Strength/]sequel[/url]. It would be too much of a work for the developers, as the game is already a success in the first place without these, anyway. 

Overall, Orwell managed to capture the feel of spying people to get info under the surface of the known. Which makes this game as one of my favorites, enough to delve deeper into privacy breach.


Be wary, always be open for possibilities.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'll admit, I was skeptical, even with all the glowing reviews on Steam. However, bored with playing the same old games, I decided to give the game a try since it wasn't even 10$. As I started up the game, I asked myself - how this game could possibly keep me interested? It's a game where you're literally staring at a 'computer' screen in-game.. when you're already staring at a computer screen in real life. Not even 10 minutes in and I was hooked. I needed more information and I needed it NOW! I got really invested in the fictional characters stories, lives and background; why did she break up with him? How long were they dating? Why is 'X's relationship with her parents so strained? I looked through every single e-mail and chat message I could find. I listened to countless phone calls and actually cared what was said and listened intently. All the while snickering to myself because the fictional characters didn't know I was listening in on their conversations. 

This game proves that sometimes being innovative and creative pays off. The game was worth every last dollar. It's relatively short (6 hours) and  I played all the episodes straight through, but it still managed to keep me excited and interest throughout the whole game. I kept playing 'just 10 more minutes' to find new information. Although only 6 hours long, I felt like it's the perfect length. Any longer and I probably would have started getting annoyed (because I did want to find out the ending to the story). 

The only issues I had with the game was that it doesn't really explain how the 'upload information' works. It tells you very briefly what your job is - to upload information, but I didn't understand that I could literally choose what information to upload and what to withold. I thought I had to upload certain information to continue with the story - turns out that may not have necessarily been the case. I actually got an ending I didn't intend because even at the end of the game I wasn't really sure what I was supposed to be doing (how did I access information, not upload it but still continue with the story?). You would think 'upload information' would be an easy concept to understand and wouldn't really need a tutorial, but in my case I would have liked a proper 2-3 minute introduction to how Orwell 'works'. The fact that you can choose what you do and do not upload, and depending on that - there will be different concequences. 
The highlighting of relevant text kinda made the game too easy, but I do understand the necessity of the function. Any real-life program such as Orwell would probably have a similar feature that highlights relevant information. I felt like it made the game more realistic because occassionally while reading an on-going chat, I could quickly scan for relevant information that was highlighted - upload it - and then continue reading the conversation. 
I really idn't realize that my actions of uploading certain information would have concequences; I guess I thought the game was a lot more linear, not that I could actually influence what happened by what I did or did not upload. 

This was really unique, both in game-playstyle as well as story telling. I'll be playing it again, that's for sure.

You would think 'upload information' would be an easy concept to understand and wouldn't really need a tutorial, but in my case I would have liked a proper 2-3 minute introduction to how Orwell 'works'. The fact that you can choose what you do and do not upload, and depending on that - there will be different concequences. The highlighting of relevant text kinda made the game too easy, but I do understand the necessity of the function. Any real-life program such as Orwell would probably have a similar feature that highlights relevant information. I felt like it made the game more realistic because occassionally while reading an on-going chat, I could quickly scan for relevant information that was highlighted - upload it - and then continue reading the conversation. I really idn't realize that my actions of uploading certain information would have concequences; I guess I thought the game was a lot more linear, not that I could actually influence what happened by what I did or did not upload. This was really unique, both in game-playstyle as well as story telling. I'll be playing it again, that's for sure.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
GENERAL OVERVIEW
Awesome game and "out-of-the-box" genre. Gameplay is very interesting since you analyze the suspects from a digital device, without physically following them. You get to know every small aspects of their lives, but this is a factor that greatly complicates the developer's work. For the ones who love the detective genre, this one is a very good choice. But I can't give a fully positive opinion on this: let's start with the upsides.
PROS
1)Rich and deep story. Keeps the gamer interested.
2)Orwell system is very well structured, its display is simple and not effort-requiring.
3)Plot-twists excluded, the game is actually chill. It keeps you concentrated, but not nervous or stressed. The fact that you can sit down and think of your next move, gives the game the right pace.
CONS
1)Low graphic and audio impact. Although the story keeps the gamer focused, that is probably the only one factor. I dare to say the game has a poor multimedial content. Characters don't "say" a single word for all the story.. You just hear music and other minor sound effects.
2)Too often it remains unclear where "the game finishes and the gamer starts". Has it ever happened to you that you can't understand how heavy will your decision be on your remaining gameplay? It happens too many times in Orwell. It's not clear when your action will bring to irreversible consequences, and this is annoying. Sometimes it feels like the game is playing you, and this is boring because the plot does not prompt the player to take important actions.
3)Insufficiently exhaustive tutorial. Although Orwell is pretty much a game with a "simple dynamic", basically gathering relevant information, I think that the small tutorial in the beginning does not clarify enough what the Orwell system is about. Even though in the tutorial-phase of the game is explained how you should deal with Orwell, the gamer fully grasps the concept after some time, and this is not acceptable in a game where choices matter (especially in one where it's not clear where choices are supposed to be made!). I came from hundreds of detective-genre games but this one is different, the developer knows, so maybe they should have stressed the basic principle more.
4)Lack of languages. This is a text-adventure. There should be plenty of available languages! I understand that this would be an incredibly long job... But this is a noticeable downside. This is quite a problem for non-natives english speakers, and a barrier for non english speakers.
5) You gather information on this system called Orwell, but as you go on with the game, you may find out more precise details, or that the information you considered relevant are just circumstancial. This is a normal day in the life of an investigator. So, why can't the player modify the datachunks relating to characters' pages? this is a forcing. A super complex system like Orwell doesn't allow the investigator to cancel what he wrote?
OVERALL OPINION
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a very nice game, that will be appreciated by most of the detective-games community. It's passionating, you would never desire it to end, it makes you feel a real investigator. Nevertheless, it has noteworthy downsides and there's a wide improvement margin under some aspects. Recommended.

review_text_raw:
This review is spoiler-free.

I picked up Orwell because I love games that put you in the role of a detective. I previously played "Her Story" and hoped this would be along similar lines (albeit with a different interface), going through data and gaining clues in order to pinpoint suspects.

After playing the game, I was left fairly satisfied and definitely had an enjoyable experience with it, though I did find it lacking in some areas.

The good:
I loved the unique art style, and the whole set up of how you feel like you're logging on to this system as a detective. The music is great and very suitable for the game too, changing in tone dramatically when something in the game changes. I love the overall Orwell theme and how it makes you think about things like government surveillance and whether it's a good or a bad thing. The characters were fairly interesting to me (though mostly unlikable, but that may have been the idea). I enjoyed the way the game is structured and how gathering certain bits of data about a person unlocks more data such as relevant URLs or documents.  I found it intriguing and I wanted to keep on playing after each chapter (there are five chapters in total).

The bad:
The game is pretty short, lasting about five hours, however I do feel like the price point is good for the experience you get. 
I felt like the mechanics of investigation had some excellent ideas but that they could have gone further with it. The game always highlighted where new information was available, and although I suppose that did stop you sifting through all the old documents you had, I kinda wanted to have to do that sifting - as a detective might. It felt a bit too hand-holding as to showing you where to look next, and sometimes that just made it feel like I was just following a path of "look at the new informatiion", "drag it to the person's profile", "look at the new bit of information"... and so on. I think maybe if it wasn't always so obvious which information to go back to, it would have been more fun to find it yourself.

I think in general, I just wanted more of the game, it was definitely a good start, but I would love to see more chapters, or a new story. And maybe an option to not have the right bits of data or documents highlighted, so you had to figure some more stuff out yourself. I think then I would have felt like a more clever detective! 

But all in all, I enjoyed the way the story wrapped up, and a lot of the ideas and mechanics, such as deciding between conflicting information, deciding what to submit and what to ignore to determine what light you put somebody in.. and I enjoyed the end of the game too. 

I think it's a 7/10 for me, an all-round good experience, but lacking in some areas that could have made it more fun/satisfying.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I absolutely recommend this game wholeheartedly; it's been over a year since I've been this immersed and emotionally invested into a game.  The game makes a point, but it's never heavy-handed about it; I really appreciate that, since too many stories of this nature is ruined by the author's soapbox.  The short pool of characters, and the fact that you are digging into aspects of their lives, learning information that they wouldn't tell anyone else, results in a special level of investment in the world.

It's nice to see a game where your choices do actually matter; the story branches out depending on what you do.  And while it does follow the same parallels, and generally tie back into itself at the end, it's not in such a way that negates the choices you've made up until that point.  The link between your choices and the results is usually sensical, and generally tied to how diligent you are in the game as opposed to needing a guide or crystal ball.  Usually, anyways; there is one situation where doing an objectively better job leads to an objectively worse result and (to me) felt like it should have been avoidable if I had just done better, but nope.  It's a fly in the ointment, but it's not bad enough to spoil the obvious care that's gone into this game.

There are a couple more minor niggles here and there; for example, I wish the game made it more clear that the information above a submittable piece of information is exactly what gets added, as opposed to a summary.  Relatedly, make it clear that they act on the information given without outside context.  This being unclear at the beginning tripped me up a couple times.

It's amazing how internally consistent the game is; nothing happens out of the blue, and if you look back (or on a second playthrough), you can see the events in retrospect.  The in-game rules aren't broken, either.  It's actually rather impressive.

The only major downside I can think of to the game is the general lack of replay value.  The first time through, you'll probably take about five hours or so.  The second time would be to go back and see everything as it occurs with the benefit on knowing the truth, plus more achievements.  Another playthrough or two after that to mop up achievements, if you really want to.  The game has no way of restarting the current day, or from a previous day, and only has one save file that overwrites itself automatically after every choice you make, so most of your time in subsequent playthroughs will be watching conversations that can't be skipped or sped up.

On balance with the replay value, and the skill and care that went into the game, I'd definitely say it's worth the ten dollar price point.  As I said at the start, it's a game that's had me more enthralled than any game I've played in the last year.  If you like this sort of thing, definitely give it a shot.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell has definitely made it onto my list of indie favorites. One of the most interesting and engaging games I've played in a long time.

[b]Story[/b]
The story and characters are well written, realistic, and relatable. The pacing is perfect and each chapter will leave you anxious to get into the next one. The world has depth and lives and breathes. Your actions feel as though they carry real weight with consequences that follow you. This is the sort of story that you'll think about and speculate about even when you're not playing. It's obvious a lot of thought was put into Orwell.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
I think it's fair to say Orwell is more of an interactive novel than a game. But that by no means is a mark against it.

Gameplay is simple but effective. You play as an investigator trying to solve a recent bombing using whatever online information, public or private, is made available to you. When you come across information that your system (named Orwell) recognizes as relevant to one of your target persons, it becomes highlighted and you can choose to upload it to Orwell's database where your superiors can then see it and act on it.

But this surveillance system isn't perfect. Sometimes conflicting or irrelevant information will be highlighted and you'll have to use your best judgement when choosing what to upload. I won't explain more in depth than that - I think the rest of the gameplay is best experienced when you discover it yourself. But I promise the gameplay isn't the mindless drag and drop that it might seem.

And what I thought was neat is that while some aspects of the gameplay might seem arbitrary or slightly confusing at first, these mechanics have a real canon, in-world explanation that is revealed as you progress. The gameplay really feels like part of the story here.

[b]Performance[/b]
It'll probably run on just about anything.

[b]Length[/b]
There are five chapters, each of which took me 45-60 minutes or so. Some people might complete it faster since I'm the methodical, read-everything-before-moving-on sort (which is rewarding with Orwell). Very little (if any) replay value though. Some people might recommend playing it all in one sitting, but I would say taking day or two long breaks like I did is the way to go.

[b]Price[/b]
Full price at the time of this review is $10. I was able to grab Orwell while it was temporarily free. $10 seems a little bit steep at first, but considering the ~5 hours I got out of it and the impression it left on me, I would say Orwell is easily worth that much. You can probably also count on Orwell going on sale or getting it cheap in a bundle if you're still on the fence.

[b]Conclusion[/b]
Get it. If you enjoy indie games, get it. If you like a good detective story, get it. If surveillance or digital privacy even remotely interest you (which they should), get it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I saw someone complaining that they didn't enjoy the game because it asks for an email address at the start. I would like to point out that this is optional and has no effect on the game, at all.


Pros:

- I love 1984 and obviously this game is heavily inspired by it.
- Relaxing gameplay.
- Thought-provoking story, especially as we seem to be moving towards a world of 'alternative facts' and other Orwellian concepts in real life.
- Game is long enough that I felt like I got my money's worth, but not so long that it started to get boring and overstay its welcome.
- Seems to have enough replay value for at least two playthroughs.
- Is not too heavy-handed with the anti-surveillance message. Clearly that is the point of the game, but they don't treat you like an idiot with it.
- Some of the choices do require actual thought and planning to make the right choice.
- Consequences for making the wrong choices.
 
Cons:

- In my opinion, the artsyle is a bit too 'whimsical' for the plot of the game. They seemed at odds with one another most of the time.
- It would have been nice if there had been some voice acting. I didn't mind that most of the game was just text, but when listening on phonecalls it would have been nice for them to have been voiced with subtitles.
- The story is extremely linear where one piece of located text triggers the next event and nothing will happen until you find it. Once you realize this it does take some of the urgency out of the game. It would be nice if things like IM chats and phone calls happened whether you were ready or not, so that there could be some threat of you missing information or getting swamped.
- The game holds your hand the entire way. When I first booted it up I thought that I was in a tutorial segment and that a while the highlighting around relevant text and the constant prodding from your supervisor would slow down, but they don't. Every bit of important information is highlighted for you already, so you really don't have to read anything if you don't want to. In a way the game will play itself in a way. There are times when you can choose the wrong info and get scolded, but I found that 95% of the time you just upload whatever data Orwell has already highlighted for you. It eliminates the biggest part of the gameplay, in my opinion. I think the game would have benefitted a lot from taking a Papers, Please approach where you have to scour the data and decide what you think is important and your supervisor chimes in every now and then to punish or praise you, depending.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game f*cked with my mind. Oh heavenly gods of nerddom, did it ever. Gather round, boys and girls, as I tell you why:

Orwell takes place in a country called "The Nation" (obviously not to be confused with anything casually tyrannical like "The Empire"). The political ruling party, The Party (much imaginative), has come into power and, thanks to the newly created office of the Secretary of Security, has in the last few years passed a Safety Bill meant to protect The Nation from any and every individual(s) who pose a threat to national security (think of the Patriot Act as a IRL equivalent). And just like NSA wiretapping, the Safety Bill gives the government dubious leeway to monitor suspected individuals through various channels (i.e., social media, email, phone calls, text messages, etc). The computer program the government employs to collect and complie such information is ironically named "Orwell" and you are hired as an Orwell investigator to track down a group of suspected individuals believed to be responsible for a series of bombings that have occurred in The Nation's capitol city of Bonton (ridiculous name I have to say, I couldn't stop thinking of bonbons). As an investigator you are paired with an adviser through whom you pass information on to higher channels who take the appropriate action. Although you are given objectives whose completion is information-dependent, it becomes ultimately clear that you, the investigator, your judgement, your discerning eye, your evaluation of possible repercussions of all the information at your fingertips, is what drives the game. The endgame of Orwell depends on you and your choices. Will you do the right thing, whatever you believe is the right thing? 

Aesthetics-wise, this game is just pretty damn near pleasing. It's a simple point-and-click with elegant yet simple graphics. The attention to detail is great, from the texts to the functionality of Orwell itself. The whole feel of the game, especially at certain moments (I'm not going to be a no-good, spoiley spoilsport), makes one forget that this is JUST A SIMULATION, NOT REAL LIFE CALM THE F*CK DOWN. I will say it's easy to get overwhelmed by the sheer density of information and how to appropriately navigate, in terms of the expected outcome. But hey, maybe it's a personal thing. I am more used to FPS than this sort of genre of game. 

In conclusion: PLAY THE GAME, FAM. DO IT. JUST DO IT!

It's a simple point-and-click with elegant yet simple graphics. The attention to detail is great, from the texts to the functionality of Orwell itself. The whole feel of the game, especially at certain moments (I'm not going to be a no-good, spoiley spoilsport), makes one forget that this is JUST A SIMULATION, NOT REAL LIFE CALM THE F*CK DOWN. I will say it's easy to get overwhelmed by the sheer density of information and how to appropriately navigate, in terms of the expected outcome. But hey, maybe it's a personal thing. I am more used to FPS than this sort of genre of game. In conclusion: PLAY THE GAME, FAM. DO IT. JUST DO IT!

review_text_raw:
I got this game for free through humble bundle during the giveaway period so I thought "Ehh, why not?".

I was genuinely surprised. This game is SO DAMN GOOD.
I'm still at chapter 3 of the game but I'll update this once I finish it.
So, here's a detailed rundown so far:

Story:
The game starts out with a cinematic that introduces the world and how it advanced it is in terms of technology. You will play as a rookie investigator of sorts who will undergo a basic test of performance. Here, it lays out your role and responsibilities clearly without being overly confusing. After all the introductions, the actual story starts. The story is INTENSE. It tries to confuse you but you want more of it. And the urge just doesn't stop until you get clearance. Especially where your choices matter.

Characters:
The characters feel alive. You can tell that a lot of work has been put into these characters as you get to know their backgrounds, way of thinking, motives, goals, etc. Heck, I even relate and sympathize with some of these characters.

Sound:
Sometimes so relaxing like you had a good day at work. Sometimes so intense that you want to scream "Damn this scroll bar!!!!11" as you race against time scrolling down frantically looking the datachunk (piece of information) in hopes that it may change the potential outcome. Sometimes grim when you find out secrets that the characters themselves never mentions.

UI:
I love the simplistic yet futuristic UI design and world setting. It helps keep you immersed in the game which revolves around you, the player, acting as an investigator from when you start the game and through your whole playthrough.

Overall:
Still on the edge of my seat while writing this review. This game is very well-made. The world is solidly built, the characters feel alive, the soundtrack enhances the gameplay, and the UI fits into the setting extremely well. If you have played hacknet, emily is away, or similar games, then this game shares a resemblance to those. It's a very personal experience and a very pleasant one at that.


Is the game worth it? If you like immersing yourself in stories, absolutely.
Then again, this is just my personal opinion on the game and it is in no way true for everyone. 
You may find this lacking if narrative games aren't your thing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a difficult one! The premise and the story are both quite complicated and intelligently woven. However, the execution is less so. This game suffers from the very same type of problems that LA Noire did: how to make a detective/analysis game without too little or too much handholding.

The idea of the investigative software is quite well-written; and depending on your ending, has a lot of payoffs. But the fact that the software pinpoints what it thinks is important and relevant kinda breaks the realism and limits a lot of your options. A lot of times, decisions that you make won't have the intended consequences and not because "life is complicated" or "shit happens" but because that's now how you linguistically interpreted the data. And that is the limitation of every game that has attempted to use language as a mechanic. There are still too many unknowns and interpretations to be able to identify and script every possible `effect` after you've set a `cause`.


Of course, there's no undo or rollback so you have to keep going with what you've done so far. The concept of `conflicting info` is also weird and unrealistic. Sometimes, it warns you that this info conflicts with some other info that you haven't even loaded or read. How does the software know that?! I realize that this aspect of analysis needs to be "gamefied" but that's where this game shows its greatest weakness. It's as if the software is already run by an AI and you just need to answer a few multiple choice questions here and there.

There's also a number of annoying UI issues like notifications. I kept gettings notifications for new or unread articles when I had accessed them and read them numerous times. Same with the datachunk notification. And when you're hunting for something specific towards the end of the game, and you have a ton of data, those icons can get downright annoying and misleading forcing you to skim and scroll through heaps of useless articles.

Still, the game and the story have a lot to say about our current society and it's definitely worth a replay for things you might have missed the first time. Not to mention that it has multiple endings.

The music's quite good too!

This is where the similarities end, as [i]you are not the attorney in this[/i]. You are the [i]judge, jury, and executioner[/i]. It is up to you to interpret where things go. You have an aide, but they do nothing for you. You give them the information, and they act upon it. It is clear, however, that they do have some opinions on whatever information you find. They will accept most of it without question, and I'm fairly sure the only information they will not accept is entirely within the first episode, which serves as a tutorial.
